title: How to work a three-quarter cross-stitch
subtitle: The curve-softening stitch for rounded outlines
excerpt: A three-quarter cross-stitch combines the full lower diagonal with a half-diagonal that terminates at the centre of the Aida square. It is the stitch that softens edges and suggests curves in a grid-based medium. Most animal and floral charts use it to round off the outline where a full square would read as a jagged step.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. The three-quarter and quarter stitch pairing is documented in Weldon's Practical Needlework (1880s), Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: The first full diagonal of a cross-stitch combined with a second half-diagonal that terminates at the centre hole of the Aida square rather than the opposite corner. This produces a triangular stitch that fits into half the square and is used to suggest curves and rounded outlines.

Only the half-diagonal that terminates at the centre of the Aida square, without the full lower diagonal of a three-quarter stitch. A quarter and a three-quarter stitch can share a single Aida square between two different colours.

Come up at the bottom-left and go down at the top-right.
Work the full lower diagonal exactly as for a full cross-stitch: bottom-left corner to top-right corner.
Bring the needle up at the bottom-right corner of the same square.
Go down at the centre hole.

Push the needle down through the hole at the exact centre of the Aida square, between the four corner holes. On standard 14-count Aida, the centre hole is clearly visible between the woven threads. This is the half-diagonal that forms the third quarter of the stitch.
Sharing a square with a quarter stitch

When a chart places two different colours in one square, one colour takes the three-quarter stitch and the other takes the quarter stitch. Work the three-quarter stitch first. Then change to the second colour and come up at the remaining corner, going down through the same centre hole. The square now holds two colours: the three-quarter stitch fills the larger triangle, the quarter stitch fills the smaller one.

Cross-stitch charts indicate three-quarter stitches with a large triangle inside the square symbol and quarter stitches with a small triangle. The direction of the triangles tells you which corner each stitch starts from. Study the chart key before starting; the triangles are tiny and easy to misread on complex charts.
